name: Greenland
summary: The world’s largest island, home of the Inuit; a Danish colony from 1721, part of Denmark from 1953, with home rule from 1979 and self-government from 2009.

location.value: Between the Arctic and Atlantic oceans; 2,166,086 km², with the ice sheet covering 81% (1,755,637 km²).

terrain.value: An ice sheet covers about 80 percent of the island, leaving a narrow rocky coastal strip with fjords.

climate.value: Arctic and subarctic, with very cold winters and cool short summers.

resources.value: Fish and shrimp, which are most of the exports, plus minerals (rare earths, zinc, gold) and hydropower.

disasters.value: The melting ice sheet is raising sea levels, and landslide-triggered waves (tsunamis) have hit some villages.

population.value: 56,831 (2025 estimate, infobox); the body gives 56,542 for 2025 and 56,583 for 2022.

urbanisation.value: Nuuk is the capital and largest town; most people live in a few towns along the south-west coast.

disease.value: Tuberculosis was a serious problem in the 1900s, and European diseases hit Inuit communities after contact.

migration.value: Many young people move to Denmark for study or work; Greenlandic Inuit came from Arctic Canada about 1,000 years ago.

economicBase.value: Fishing is over 90% of exports. Danish aid averaged 5.4 billion kroner a year in 2019–23 (over 20% of GDP); the 2024 block grant was 4.3 billion kroner, about a third of public revenue. Shrimp and halibut are not named.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade runs by sea and air, mostly with Denmark; shipping is closed by ice in many months.

wealth.value: The article says GDP per person is equivalent to that of the average economies of Europe; it does not use the term “high income”. HDI 0.852 (very high, 52nd).

moneyAndTax.value: The Danish krone, plus an annual block grant from Denmark.

inequality.value: A gap exists between the towns and the small, remote settlements, and between Greenlandic and Danish residents.

governmentType.value: A self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark; self-rule gained on 21 June 2009.

keyRulers.value: Jonathan Motzfeldt, first premier (1979), is not named in the part of the page read. Present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Elections for the Inatsisartut (parliament); the head of state is the Danish monarch.

institutions.value: Inatsisartut (the parliament) and the Naalakkersuisut (the government), under Danish sovereignty.

stability.value: Politically stable, with peaceful debate about independence.

eliteConflict.value: Debate over independence from Denmark, and about how to use mineral wealth and tourism.

armyAndTech.value: Defence by Denmark; US Pituffik (Thule) base.

majorWars.value: Not confirmed. The part of the page read does not cover the Second World War; it describes Pituffik Space Base as a US territorial concession in perpetuity.

territoryChange.value: The island’s borders have not changed; Norway’s claim to East Greenland was ruled against by the court in 1933.

alliancesRivals.value: Left the European Community in 1985 after a vote in 1982; the United States has a base at Pituffik (Thule).

inventions.value: Inuit developed the kayak, the umiak, the harpoon and cold-weather clothing, suited to the Arctic.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Greenland in Nuuk, and a major centre for ice and climate research.

openness.value: Denmark closed the island to outsiders until 1950, but it is now open to trade and tourists.

communicationTransport.value: Planes, boats, dog sleds; no roads between towns.

religion.value: Lutheran Christianity (about 95.5% in the infobox; 91% were church members in 2025). The page describes Hans Egede's expedition of 1721 as part of Dano-Norwegian colonisation.

languageWriting.value: Greenlandic (Kalaallisut) declared the sole official language in 2009.

artsArchitecture.value: Drum dancing, tupilak carvings and colourful wooden houses.

socialStructure.value: Paleo-Inuit entered about 2500 BC; the Thule culture, ancestors of today’s Greenlanders, arrived around 1300. Inuit are 89.5% of the population (2020).

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Inuit and Greenlandic identity; Kalaallisut is the official language.

dailyLife.value: People live in small coloured wooden houses, eat seal, fish and reindeer, and travel by boat, dog sled or plane.

neighbours.value: Canada (across the narrow Nares Strait), Iceland and Svalbard.

ideasReligions.value: Inuit traditions with spirits of the sea and sky, and Lutheran Christianity since the 1700s.

colonisation.value: Norse settlement from 986; the 1953 Constitution of Denmark ended Greenland’s colonial status.

riseSignals.value: Home rule: referendum on 17 January 1979; the law took effect on 1 May 1979.

declineSignals.value: None; it is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.

outcome.value: A self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, recognised as a separate people under international law.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
